title: Haaland’s Late Winner Sends Norway Past Ivory Coast and Into a World Cup Showdown With Brazil
excerpt: The Manchester City striker scored his fifth goal of the tournament in the 86th minute, securing Norway’s first-ever knockout win at a World Cup — and setting up a rematch 28 years in the making.
body:
ARLINGTON, Texas — For 85 minutes at AT&T Stadium, Erling Haaland was practically invisible. Ivory Coast’s backline had done what so few defenders manage: they kept the most prolific striker on the planet quiet. Then came the 86th minute.

Substitute Oscar Bobb surged down the right flank and threaded a pass to Patrick Berg inside the penalty area. Berg’s cross took a slight deflection, but it didn’t matter. There was Haaland — wide open, five yards out, doing what he always does. The ball barely crossed the line, more a prod than a strike, but it was enough. Norway 2, Ivory Coast 1. Pandemonium in north Texas.

“Keep dreaming,” Haaland had written on social media the night before the match. By full time, he had turned that dream into something tangible — Norway’s first-ever knockout-stage victory at a World Cup.

## A match of three acts

The game had followed a familiar World Cup script: tension, breakthrough, and late drama.

Norway took control in the first half through Antonio Nusa, whose curling left-footed strike in the 39th minute bent into the top corner and silenced the Ivorian contingent in the 70,000-seat stadium. It was a goal of genuine quality from the RB Leipzig winger, cutting inside from the left before finding the far post with surgical precision.


![Patrick Berg — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c3/Norway_Italy_-_June_2025_A_14_%28cropped%29.jpg)



> **"“Keep dreaming,” Haaland had written on social media the night before the match."**



But Ivory Coast, reigning Africa Cup of Nations champions, were never going to go quietly. In the 74th minute, Amad Diallo — introduced as a substitute just minutes earlier — collected the ball on the right, embarked on a mazy run through three Norwegian defenders, and lashed a left-footed shot past goalkeeper Ørjan Nyland. The Manchester United winger’s individual brilliance had pulled the Elephants level and set up a frantic final quarter.

For a stretch, extra time looked inevitable. Then Bobb, Berg, and Haaland combined to script the winner with four minutes of regular time remaining.

Even after Haaland’s goal, the drama wasn’t finished. In the 96th minute, Diallo stepped up to take a free kick from 25 yards, curling a shot destined for the top corner. Nyland threw himself to his right and clawed it behind for a corner with one hand — a save that will live alongside the goal in Norwegian football folklore.

## Fastest to 60

Haaland’s tap-in was his fifth goal of the tournament and his 60th for Norway in just 53 appearances — making the Manchester City striker the fastest player in the history of international football to reach that milestone. He has now scored in 13 consecutive competitive matches for his country, netting 25 goals in that extraordinary run.

The 25-year-old Manchester City striker has finished as the English Premier League’s top scorer in three of the four seasons since his move from Borussia Dortmund in 2022. But it is at this World Cup, playing in front of adoring crowds on American soil, where he has elevated his legend to another level entirely: two goals against Iraq, two against Senegal, and now the late winner that put Norway into the Round of 16.


![World Cup — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fb/Kitzbuehel_slalom_ganslernhang_2010.jpg)


## Twenty-eight years in the waiting

For Norwegian football, this victory is generational. The country had not appeared at a World Cup since 1998 — when a squad featuring Tore André Flo and Ole Gunnar Solskjær pulled off one of the greatest upsets in tournament history, beating reigning champions Brazil 2-1 in the group stage in Marseille.

Now, 28 years later, fate has arranged a sequel. Norway will face five-time champions Brazil in the Round of 16 on Sunday, July 5, at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. The venue is the same ground where Norway beat Senegal 3-2 in the group stage — and the same stadium that will host the World Cup Final on July 19.

Brazil, who edged Japan 2-1 in extra time in Houston on Monday, will present a vastly different challenge. But if Haaland’s run of form continues, no backline in the world is safe.

## The World Cup on your doorstep

For Indian Americans across the country, this World Cup has been an unprecedented chance to experience football’s grandest spectacle up close. Arlington’s DFW metroplex, home to one of the fastest-growing South Asian communities in the United States, saw Indian tricolours scattered through the stands on Tuesday — fans drawn to the sheer spectacle even without India in the field.

The Norway-Brazil clash at MetLife moves the tournament to the doorstep of the country’s largest Indian-American population. The New York-New Jersey metro area, home to more than 700,000 people of Indian descent, has already hosted five World Cup matches, with raucous, diverse crowds turning every game into a cultural event. Tickets for Sunday’s Round of 16 clash start at roughly $1,800 — a steep price, but one that hasn’t deterred fans who see this as a once-in-a-generation opportunity.

For NRIs who have spent decades adopting American sports traditions — from Super Bowl parties to NBA playoffs watch nights — the World Cup on home turf is different. This is the sport most of them grew up with, played in school, argued about at family dinners. India may not have a team in the bracket, but the World Cup on American soil has made the beautiful game feel like home. Many Indian Americans, especially those who grew up watching international football, are finding a unique connection to their roots through the tournament. The shared passion for the sport, often a topic of conversation with family back in India, strengthens cultural ties and provides a common ground for celebration, even if their home country isn't competing. This shared experience also offers a unique opportunity for the diaspora to connect with the broader American community, fostering a sense of belonging while celebrating their heritage. For many, it's a chance to introduce their American-born children to the global sport that holds such significance in their ancestral homeland, bridging generational and cultural divides. The World Cup provides a vibrant platform for the diaspora to celebrate their global identity, connecting with fellow fans from diverse backgrounds and reinforcing the universal appeal of football.

*Norway play Brazil in the Round of 16 on Sunday, July 5, at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. Kick-off is at 4 p.m. ET / 1 p.m. PT. The match airs on FOX, with streaming on Fubo and Peacock.*
